ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Progress Note 2 — Focused Visit (Follow-up) — Lili Boulanger

code.originalText: Diagnosis of Crohn disease with intestinal tuberculosis excluded; inflammatory bowel disease consultation the same day

text.paragraph: Results of colonoscopy, MR enterography, and tuberculosis tests. [S]

Ms. Boulanger returns nine days after presenting with four months of right lower abdominal cramping, loose stools up to six times a day and at night, evening fevers, and loss of 6 kg. The ileocolonoscopy five days ago showed deep longitudinal ulcers over the last 15 cm of the terminal ileum and patchy ulcers in the ascending and transverse colon with normal mucosa between and a spared rectum (SES-CD 14). The biopsies show chronic active ileitis and colitis with crypt distortion and a few small non-caseating granulomas; the acid-fast stain and TB PCR are negative and the mycobacterial culture is pending. MR enterography two days ago shows 18 cm of inflamed terminal ileum without stricture, fistula, abscess, or necrotic nodes. The interferon-gamma release assay is negative and the chest X-ray normal. Stool tests for Clostridioides difficile, bacterial pathogens, and parasites are negative, and celiac serology is negative. The pregnancy test is negative. She has five or six loose stools a day with cramping and fatigue (Harvey-Bradshaw Index 11). She met Dr. Nwankwo-Delacroix this morning and chose a treatment with him. She has a concert of her choral works in late March and asked whether she could still perform. [S]

list.item:
Crohn disease of the terminal ileum and colon, Montreal A2 L3 B1, moderate to severe (K50.80). The endoscopic pattern (long ileal ulcers, skip lesions, spared rectum), small non-caseating granulomas, and imaging fit Crohn disease. Intestinal tuberculosis, the main alternative, is very unlikely: negative interferon-gamma release assay, normal chest X-ray, no caseating or confluent granulomas, and negative acid-fast stain and TB PCR; the culture will be checked at six weeks. Her features predict a disabling course (young age, extensive and deep ulcers, weight loss), so an advanced therapy should start now rather than after other drugs fail. She was told the diagnosis directly, with what it means for her life and work. [S]
Risankizumab 600 mg intravenously at weeks 0, 4, and 8, the first infusion in five days, then 360 mg under the skin every 8 weeks; chosen by her with Dr. Nwankwo-Delacroix.
Prednisone 40 mg daily from today, reduced by 5 mg each week to stop in eight weeks, as a bridge.
Liver enzymes and bilirubin today and through at least week 12.
She can plan to perform in March; a plan for bathroom access at the venue.

Iron deficiency anemia (D50.0). Hemoglobin 10.6 and ferritin 9 with active inflammation: oral iron is poorly absorbed and can worsen symptoms. [S]
Ferric derisomaltose 1000 mg intravenously with the first risankizumab infusion; phosphate checked at the next visit.

Moderate protein-calorie malnutrition (E44.0). BMI 17.5 after a 12 percent weight loss; albumin 3.3. [S]
Dietitian seen today: small frequent meals and two oral nutritional supplements a day.
Weight at every visit.

Vitamin D deficiency, with a course of prednisone ahead (E55.9). Vitamin D 18 ng/mL; DXA today within the expected range for age (Z-scores -1.4 and -1.1). [S]
Vitamin D3 2000 units daily; calcium carbonate 1250 mg daily while on prednisone.
No repeat DXA unless steroids are needed again.
